# Diagnosing 2AZFE Idle Vibration After Mount Replacement

Replacing engine mounts on a 2009 Toyota Camry with the 2AZ-FE engine is a labor-intensive task, but it often yields immediate results regarding drivetrain vibration. In your specific case, you successfully eliminated the lurching acceleration and smoothed out driving dynamics, which indicates the original rubber was indeed degraded or separated. However, the emergence of a new symptom—a distinct idle vibration only in Drive that disappears in Neutral, Park, or Reverse—suggests the issue has shifted from pure mechanical isolation to an engine control or load-mapping problem.

When you replaced all four mounts (the three lower ones and the upper dogbone), you altered the mounting geometry and stiffness characteristics of the entire assembly. While factory parts are generally reliable, it is possible that one specific mount was defective out of the box, or more likely, the adjustment in rigidity has exposed a pre-existing idle control issue that the worn mounts previously masked. The fact that the vibration frequency matches when you turn the steering wheel left suggests the engine may be physically rocking within the bay due to uneven load distribution, but since the mounts look fine under inspection, the root cause is likely internal to the powertrain.

The primary suspect for a 2AZ-FE engine exhibiting rough idle specifically in Drive is the Throttle Position Sensor (TPS) or the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve logic. When you put the car in gear, the Transmission Range Switch sends a signal to the Powertrain Control Module (PCM). The PCM then expects the throttle plate to be at a specific "load" position (usually slightly open) to maintain idle speed under load. If the TPS calibration is off, or if there is carbon buildup preventing the IAC valve from bypassing enough air, the engine will stumble and vibrate because it cannot stabilize RPMs against the torque request of the transmission being in Drive.

Your cleaning of the throttle body was a logical step, but on the 2AZ-FE, the issue often lies deeper in the electronic calibration or the IAC motor itself. The link below provides a comprehensive guide on throttle maintenance for these generations; ensure you are checking the IAC valve stepper motor resistance and movement, not just cleaning the bore: [DIY 2AZFE Throttle Cleaning Gen 5, Gen 5.5, Gen 6](http://www.toyotanation.com/forum/104-5th-6th-generation-2002-2006-2007-2011/420994-diy-2azfe-throttle-cleaning-gen-5-gen-5-5-gen-6-a.html).

Another critical area to investigate is the wiring harness for the engine ground or sensor inputs. Vibration can sometimes be electrical in nature, caused by a loose connection that only vibrates when the engine torque fluctuates under load (Drive) but not when unloaded (Neutral/Park). Check the main relay and the grounding points near the alternator and starter motor.

Finally, consider the possibility of a defective new mount creating an imbalance. If one of the four new mounts is slightly out of spec or installed with incorrect torque, it could create a rocking motion that manifests as vibration in Drive where the engine load increases the amplitude of the oscillation. Re-checking the torque specifications on the strut tower bolts and the rear engine bracket is essential before assuming internal engine failure.
